issue_context.title: COSE_Sign1 messages (single signer) can be read, validated, and created
issue_context.body:
Implement COSE Signing, [IETF RFC 8152, section 4](https://tools.ietf.org/html/rfc8152#section-4)

## Minimum Viable Product - Single Signer

* [x] Read and expose metadata for tagged and untagged COSE_Sign1 messages
* [x] Validate signature with both embedded and detached content, from both formats.
  * [x] ECDsa
  * [x] RSASSA-PSS (from [IETF RFC 8230](https://tools.ietf.org/html/rfc8230))
* [x] Create new embedded- and detached- content signature.

This minimum viable product can be shipped as a NuGet package for verification by early adopters before continuing into the multiple signers scope.

Things that won't be covered on the MVP:
* Validation of Critical headers
* A model to interact with Counter Signatures headers.
comments:
We're using this in the wild with the EU Covid certificates; is this feature something that could figure in the coming 6-12 months? :-)

ref: https://github.com/ehn-dcc-development/hcert-spec/blob/main/hcert_spec.md

@ryanbnl We originally thought we had a highly engaged partner, then they turned out to need CBOR and one data structure from COSE, but not COSE itself, so we put this on the back burner.

The CBOR reader and writer are available: https://www.nuget.org/packages/System.Formats.Cbor.

I can't say how this will stack up against other things we want for 7, given that you're the first request for it.  It's probably not too much work (I forget how big the spec is) to make it work in your own library code, given System.Formats.Cbor and the built-in System.Security.Cryptography types.

The harder problem for us will be the classic one: coming up with public API that we're happy with.  (So far we've done not so great with SignedXml or SignedCms... third time's the charm?)

@bartonjs Would it help if I made myself the second request? We're planning to use `COSE_Sign1` as the signature format for an upcoming standard. In our C# prototype we're currently making do with the library at https://github.com/cose-wg/COSE-csharp.

Thanks for replying @bartonjs :-)

The context of this is the EU Covid Vaccination project - we've used COSE/CBOR as part of the HCERT specifications. You can find the info here:

https://github.com/ehn-dcc-development/hcert-spec

We will start to see this implemented more broadly, especially as commercial players come on to the market. For now we are using the community implementations - so we're not blocked - but it would be great to have an official implementation. Especially given that you can share a single .Net implementation over apps (Xamarin), backend (asp.net etc) and web frontend (Blazor).

The .Net implementation is here (warning: it's very much proof-of-concept code to work as a quick example):

https://github.com/ehn-dcc-development/hcert-dotnet

SignedCms: the API isn't fantastic, but there's a lot of value having good crypto support on our platform. Between the Microsoft implementations, BouncyCastle ports and libsodium wrappers there's a lot of good, but I keep hearing from the crypto experts that Go and Python are amazing because of their crypto support.
The HCERT is literally in EU law: https://eur-lex.europa.eu/legal-content/EN/TXT/?uri=CELEX%3A32021D1073 :-)

> Would it help if I made myself the second request?

Certainly doesn't hurt :smile:.

Putting a thumbs-up on the top post for the issue is helpful as it gives us a quick way to compare (however inacurately) the demand for one thing over another.

Could be interesting also at https://github.com/lumoin/Verifiable. Partially relatd to things @ryanbnl mentioned. So my thumb for CBOR too. :)

(Also that lib is still being established a few days in case someone goes to click around.)

@ryanbnl 

> SignedCms: the API isn't fantastic, but there's a lot of value having good crypto support on our platform. Between the Microsoft implementations, BouncyCastle ports and libsodium wrappers there's a lot of good, but I keep hearing from the crypto experts that Go and Python are amazing because of their crypto support.

Maybe they drop to Rust libraries undernath. Rust ecosystem seem to be where the action is. :)

I just wrote a simple wrapper to BouncyCastle, NSec and .NET libraries in https://github.com/lumoin/Verifiable. Basically the idea is an extension method with delegates (that can take `Span<byte>`) that abstract the different forms of the libraries and allow adding more libraries agnostic to these core libraries.

You can take a look if the idea is useful. This is like alpha stuff still (and other design that occurred to me could be something like `Func<Delegate, Delegate>`). Maybe this isn't the place to design. :) Sometime next week things ought to be put in place, readmes better written etc.

Nice I'll have a look! I expect this to be a growth area in the future - particularly in Europe, but also because we're seeing a lot more systems in the wild that are built on crypto. I'm certainly extremely thankful to have spent the last year and a half building cool stuff that ships to millions of people with it :)

Growth surely as things are legislated -- and .NET is lacking here a bit. :)

The crypto related is at https://github.com/lumoin/Verifiable/blob/main/test/Verifiable.Tests/CryptographicCrossTests.cs. But a noted, I move things around, add comments and that sort of things next week. I think it boils down to looking at if this idea of abstracting could work for you too (I probably add a few tests that make the library specific plumbing go unvisible too, as the idea is ultimately to rely on general signature funcs that delegate to the libraries). :)

Has the "no headers duplicated across protected & unprotected" already happened by this point?  If not, I'd do this check before the one for the protected headers.
It already happened (in the caller of this method).

Presumably this should support Span, no?  If we're holding internal references (e.g. for Content) then ReadOnlyMemory.

Of course, array overloads are also convienent.
(Since we'll have a `byte[]` overload anyways, we can just address this in the next round)

The feedback about "check how the test case is identified" applies to all `[Theory]`s.  I'm pretty sure this one will come out pretty weak.

I'd make this private, and then make three `[Fact]`s that feed into it (e.g. DuplicateProtectedHeaderThrows, DuplicateUnprotectedHeaderThrows, ProtectedAndUnprotectedHeaderThrows)
I can't easily tell from the PR... does this instance ever propagate out of the public surface area?  If yes, we should be thoughtful about it being a singleton that a consumer could modify.
It won't leak as it will be re-encoded by a `CborWriter` before returning.

This can just be:
```suggestion
        public ReadOnlyMemory<byte>? Content => _content;
```
It's a bit odd from an API perspective to have a nullable `ReadOnlyMemory<byte>`, though... is that the intention?
With your suggested syntax, the implicit operator will kick-in and the property will never return null.

> It's a bit odd from an API perspective to have a nullable ReadOnlyMemory<byte>, though... is that the intention?

it is, specially to signify a message that explicitly excluded the content (detached content as is called in the RFC). 

Also, I found some prior art in ou APIs:
https://docs.microsoft.com/en-us/dotnet/api/system.net.sockets.sendpacketselement.memorybuffer?view=net-6.0
https://docs.microsoft.com/en-us/dotnet/api/system.security.cryptography.pkcs.pkcs8privatekeyinfo.algorithmparameters?view=dotnet-plat-ext-6.0

> With your suggested syntax, the implicit operator will kick-in and the property will never return null.

Yeah, that was my question about why this is nullable.

Nullable is correct; because there's a distinction between "had empty content" (attached-empty) and "had no content" (detached), which needs to be conveyed to the caller (as it changes which Verify method they need to use)

Again, by reusing a const from the source this test is virtually guaranteed to pass.  Instead, the test should assert that it's -7, since that checks that our implementation matches the specification (from a black-box perspective)
(Since the name of this test is that it's proving a read works on an IsReadOnly map, pretend I left this comment in a place where we're checking that the algorithm ID we wrote down was correct)

I was validating the hash algorithm, you can tell by the message `Hash Algorithm '{0}' doesn't match with the specified COSE Algorithm '{1}'.` but I agree it makes more sense to validate the alg. header.

This is fine for now, but if we decide to take the partner feedback of allowing detached content to be presented as a stream (to support large detached content) we'll want to replace this with just a virtual data structure that we pipe through IncrementalHash.
NIT: probably better to apply the attribute at the type level as all membrs have it except internal constructor
Given that is a nit and the CI finished mostly clean, I will address this in a future PR.
One a second thought, we shouldn't move the attribute to the type since the internal .ctor is used in an API (`CoseMessage.DecodeSign1`) that can be called from browser.
Presumably you added this because the analyzer said to... but that seems odd... browser-compat is supposed to be opt-in, so I wouldn't expect this to trip.
Yes, the errors sprout from `ECDsa.SignData()`, `RSA.SignData()`, and `RSASignaturePadding.Pss` but I don't see any unsupported attributes in those APIs. So I don't really know what's causing them.

>  browser-compat is supposed to be opt-in, so I wouldn't expect this to trip.

That is right, by defualt it should not warn for cross platform builds, but browser team wanted to see/propogate the warning for cross-platform builds in runtime repo
If this is a value that doesn't fit in Int32 then we'll throw a COSE exception on this line, vs the CryptographicException we'd throw for it being the int.MaxValue.

On `CoseMessage.DecodeSign1`, if CborReader throws we catch the CborContentException and we throw a CryptographicException with the former being the inner exception. Perhaps we should wrap similarly with try-catch the places where we read CBOR in this and other methods.
FWIW, this was actually throwing OverflowException.
@stephentoub I feel like we started using exception filters then stopped in the subsequent release because of something to do with trimming or AoT.  Are they verboten or permissible these days?
They're fine to use.  You're probably thinking of mono AOT having an issue with them that causes it to fallback for those methods to the interpreter.
If this is a valid COSE_Sign message, consider saving it to a known value somewhere instead of having it as inline hex.
I feel like when we chatted we thought that the CoseHeaderMap parameters should be allowed to be null?  Is that just being deferred to a followup? (Or am I misremembering?)

> Is that just being deferred to a followup? 

I would prefer to defer that to a subsequent PR. It won't be a breaking change anyway.

Is there a scenario where someone knows they have the start of a COSE_Sign1 and don't know how long it is?  If so, consider `DecodeSign1(ReadOnlySpan<byte> cborPayload, out int bytesRead)` which doesn't throw on an incomplete read.
We don't have an scenario for that yet, we should probably hold off until then IMO.
